clue.text: This railway fairly has its ups and downs

definitions.text: This railway fairly has its ups and downs

parts.words: This railway fairly has its ups and downs
parts.note: a fairground railway that climbs and dips, its track literally going up and down, read as a fairground ride rather than a troubled company

explanation.surface: A railway company with a chequered history of good and bad years.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fairly' looks like 'quite', but it means 'at the fair': this is the zigzag roller-coaster railway of the fairground, whose ups and downs are literal.
explanation.definitionFit: A fairground roller coaster runs on a zigzag track that climbs and plunges, the very picture of ups and downs.

clue.text: Tearful accompaniment to an oyster-sorting

parts.note: Lewis Carroll's Walrus weeps convulsively as he sorts out the largest oysters to eat

explanation.surface: A weepy scene at a fishmonger's while the oysters are graded.
explanation.walkthrough: In Carroll's 'The Walrus and the Carpenter' the Walrus, 'with sobs and tears', sorts out the oysters of the largest size before eating them.
explanation.definitionFit: The Walrus in Carroll's poem weeps loudly, his crying heard as he picks out the oysters.

clue.text: Give him a hoe? Great Scott !

definitions.text: Give him a hoe? Great Scott !

parts.words: Give him a hoe? Great Scott
parts.note: a man's name that, with HOE added, becomes the title of a novel by the great Sir Walter Scott

explanation.surface: An exclamation of surprise at a suggestion to hand someone a garden tool.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Great Scott!' looks like an exclamation, but it points to Sir Walter Scott, whose novel takes its title from this Russian form of John plus HOE.
explanation.definitionFit: Add a hoe to this man's name and you have the title of Walter Scott's medieval romance.

clue.text: Not the easiest way to buy in bulk

definitions.text: Not the easiest way to buy in bulk

parts.words: Not the easiest way to buy in bulk
parts.note: at a wholesale warehouse you pay on the spot and haul the heavy goods away yourself

explanation.surface: A wry remark on the effort of buying large quantities.
explanation.walkthrough: At a wholesale warehouse you pay at once and take the goods away yourself, which is hard work when you are buying a lot.
explanation.definitionFit: Wholesale warehouses make shoppers pay on the spot and lug the purchases away themselves.

clue.text: Soup that's good for an Irish boy

definitions.text: Soup that's good for an Irish boy

parts.words: Soup that's good for an Irish boy
parts.note: a nourishing soup, and the Irish phrase calling a fine lively lad 'a ... of a boy'

explanation.surface: Wholesome soup recommended for a growing Irish lad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'good for' looks like 'nourishing', but it is the Irish idiom 'a broth of a boy', a fine spirited young man.
explanation.definitionFit: A thin meat or vegetable soup, and in the Irish idiom a splendid lad is called one 'of a boy'.

clue.text: Whereby church and state agree, say, not to give the plane's location

indicators.note: say signals that the words are spoken, the sound standing for different letters

parts.words: not to give the plane's location
parts.note: announcing where the supersonic airliner is, 'Concorde at ...', but stopping before naming the place

explanation.surface: A treaty between church and state, with an aside about keeping an aircraft's whereabouts secret.
explanation.walkthrough: Spoken aloud, the answer sounds like 'Concorde at...', the start of giving the airliner's location with the place itself left out.
explanation.definitionFit: A formal treaty between the Pope and a government settling the Church's position in that country.

clue.text: Dreamy fairy — woolgathering again ?

definitions.meaning: one of Titania's fairy attendants in Shakespeare's A Midsummer Night's Dream is called by this name
woolgathering usually means daydreaming, but here it is taken literally: an insect whose larvae eat wool

explanation.walkthrough: 'woolgathering' looks like daydreaming, which fits 'Dreamy', but it is the clothes insect literally gathering wool; 'Dreamy' points to the Dream, Shakespeare's play.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's Dream gives the fairy attendant named after the insect, and the clothes pest feeds on woollens.

clue.text: Ring-enlarger? Open the yellow pages, lass

parts.note: ope is a poetic form of open
a rag is a cheap newspaper, and the yellow press is sensational journalism

explanation.surface: Advice to a girl to open the telephone directory, with a puzzle about enlarging a ring.
explanation.walkthrough: 'yellow pages' is not the directory but the sensational yellow press, a rag. 'Ring' is Wagner's opera cycle, which these binoculars make look bigger.
explanation.definitionFit: Small binoculars used in the theatre magnify the stage, such as a performance of Wagner's Ring cycle.

clue.text: Knowing when to say Nay "?

parts.note: common sense about refusing, and the knowledge of an animal that neighs

explanation.surface: Wisdom about when to refuse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nay' sounds like a neigh, so the shrewdness of knowing when to refuse becomes the good sense of an animal that neighs.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain practical good judgment is called this, as if a stable animal had it.

clue.text: Money sure converted the captain

parts.note: brass is old slang for money
bound, as in 'bound to happen', means sure or certain

explanation.surface: Some money, it is said, won the captain over to the cause.
explanation.walkthrough: 'converted' reads as persuading, but it only links the money and certainty pieces to the captain they make up. A captain's uniform is trimmed with brass buttons and braid, and the word also means rigidly conventional.
explanation.definitionFit: A ship's captain in full uniform is decked out with brass buttons and fittings, hence brass-bound.

clue.text: Devon village drink

definitions.meaning: A fishing village on the coast of Devon, a county in south-west England
ale or lager, a brewed alcoholic drink

explanation.definitionFit: The Devon coastal village shares its name with the brewed drink served in pubs.

clue.text: Entering the Goodwins, for instance, pick a vessel that's new, neat

indicators.note: one piece entering another goes inside it, so the pick is placed within the sandbanks

parts.note: the Goodwin Sands are notorious sandbanks off the coast of Kent in south-east England
a pan is a cooking vessel

explanation.surface: Sailing onto the Goodwin Sands, choose a boat that is brand new and tidy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'vessel' suggests a ship near the Goodwins, a shipwreck graveyard off Kent, but it is a cooking pan; 'Entering' says the pick goes inside the sandbanks.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase first meant brand new and now means spotlessly clean and tidy.

clue.text: It shows the style is the man

definitions.text: It shows the style is the man

parts.words: It shows the style is the man
parts.note: an illustration displaying the latest clothes, and also a person whose clothes are their whole identity, echoing Buffon's saying 'the style is the man'

explanation.surface: A remark about writing, quoting the French maxim that a writer's style reveals their character.
explanation.walkthrough: Buffon's 'le style est l'homme même' is about literary style; here 'style' means clothes, and the answer is both a picture showing the fashions and a person who is all about dress.
explanation.definitionFit: A fashion illustration shows the current style, and the phrase also names a dandy whose clothing defines him.

clue.text: The old pipe's brought out each summer

indicators.note: brought out suggests the letters are taken out and laid in a fresh arrangement

explanation.surface: Grandfather's old pipe is taken out every summer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'brought out' rearranges EACH SUMMER.
explanation.definitionFit: A tobacco pipe with a bowl carved from a soft white clay mineral was a traditional smoker's favourite.

clue.text: That half-warmed fish for example

parts.note: a swapped-initials version of 'that half-formed wish', attributed to the Oxford don William Spooner

explanation.surface: A dish of lukewarm fish offered as an illustration.
explanation.walkthrough: 'half-warmed fish' is 'half-formed wish' with initial sounds swapped, the slip credited to Rev. William Spooner of Oxford.
explanation.definitionFit: Swapping the initial sounds of 'half-formed wish' gives the classic example of the slip named after Spooner.

clue.text: Export brief prepared for publication and rushed through

parts.note: EXP is the short form of export
a text made ready for printing has been edited

explanation.surface: An export document was prepared for printing and hurried through the system.
explanation.definitionFit: To hasten a process is to speed it through, so something hurried along has been sped up.

clue.text: They come to terms with the goodies

definitions.text: They come to terms with the goodies

parts.words: They come to terms with the goodies
parts.note: boarding-school pupils' boxes of treats that arrive at the start of each school term

explanation.surface: People reaching an agreement with the good guys.
explanation.walkthrough: 'come to terms' is not agreeing: these boxes arrive for the school term full of goodies; tuck is British school slang for sweets and snacks.
explanation.definitionFit: A British boarder takes a box of sweets and snacks to school at the start of term.

clue.text: Classically crooked girl? .

parts.note: a girl from Greek pastoral romance who carries a shepherd's crook, not a dishonest one

explanation.surface: A girl who was a criminal in the classical age.
explanation.walkthrough: 'crooked' suggests dishonest, but it means 'carrying a crook': in Longus's Greek romance Daphnis and Chloe the heroine is a shepherdess.
explanation.definitionFit: The heroine of the ancient Greek pastoral romance is a shepherdess, so a classical girl with a crook.

clue.text: … and one who reverts to trouble by the hour

indicators.note: reverts means turns back, so the pieces that follow are read in the opposite direction

parts.note: ado means fuss or trouble

explanation.surface: Following on from the previous clue, another girl who keeps going back to trouble by the hour.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis carries the 'girl' of 17 across into 'one'. 'reverts' turns ADO + HR into the name, and 'by the' only joins the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Continuing from the previous clue, 'one' stands for another girl, and Rhoda is a girl's name.

clue.text: Weapons advocated by misogynists

definitions.meaning: short curved swords once used by sailors and pirates
read as two words, a woman-hater's call to slash girls

explanation.walkthrough: Split as 'cut lasses', the swords become a woman-hater's slogan.
explanation.definitionFit: Pirates' curved swords are cutting weapons, and split in two the word is a call to wound girls, which a woman-hater might urge.

clue.text: It seems Miss Pecksniff does not take the Brand X liqueur

parts.note: Charity Pecksniff, daughter of the hypocrite in Dickens's Martin Chuzzlewit, is nicknamed Cherry

indicators.note: the brand does not take its last letter X, so another letter stands in its place

parts.note: the brand name as written, the letters of its two parts

explanation.surface: Dickens's Miss Pecksniff turns down an unnamed brand of liqueur.
explanation.walkthrough: 'does not take the' X of 'Brand X': the X gives way to Y, the letter after it, as in algebra. Cherry is Charity Pecksniff's pet name in Dickens's Martin Chuzzlewit.
explanation.definitionFit: A sweet cordial flavoured with cherries is a classic after-dinner liqueur.

clue.text: Out-of-the-way plea

parts.note: a defence claim that the accused was somewhere else, away from the scene of the crime

explanation.surface: An unusual or remote kind of appeal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Out-of-the-way' looks like 'remote', but it means being elsewhere; the word is Latin for 'elsewhere'.
explanation.definitionFit: A defendant's claim of being elsewhere when the crime was committed.

clue.text: Trouble with the lid ?

parts.note: the lid is the eyelid, and the trouble is an inflamed swelling on it

explanation.surface: A jar or pot whose cover will not come off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lid' suggests a pot cover; it is the eyelid, and the trouble is a small painful swelling at its edge.
explanation.definitionFit: An inflamed gland on the edge of the eyelid is a common eye complaint.

clue.text: Girl detailed in 15

indicators.note: detailed here means cut off at the tail, so the name loses its last letter

parts.note: Edith is a girl's name

explanation.surface: A young woman described at length in clue 15.
explanation.walkthrough: 'detailed' is not 'described closely' but 'with the tail docked', removing H. The four letters also sit inside the answer to 15 across, which the definition 'in 15' points to.
explanation.definitionFit: The answer to 15 across, rushed through, contains these four letters, and to prepare a text for printing is its meaning there.

clue.text: It's not only love the world goes round on !

definitions.text: It's not only love the world goes round on !

parts.words: It's not only love the world goes round on
parts.note: plays on the saying that love makes the world go round: the earth literally spins on an imaginary line through its poles

explanation.surface: A twist on the saying that love makes the world go round.
explanation.walkthrough: The saying is that love makes the world go round; literally, the earth rotates about a line through its poles.
explanation.definitionFit: The earth rotates about an imaginary line through the North and South Poles, the pivot of its spin.

clue.text: It's rooted out. That's re paid text revision

indicators.note: a revision reworks a text, so these letters are recast in a new order

explanation.surface: A note on a text that has been rooted out, revised after being paid for again.
explanation.walkthrough: 'revision' rearranges RE PAID TEXT; 'It's' and 'That's' only link.
explanation.definitionFit: To pull something out by the roots is to eradicate it, the literal sense of this Latin-derived word.

clue.text: Take off the mining engineer

definitions.meaning: to take off someone is to mimic or imitate them
M.I.Min.E. style letters, Member of the Institution of Mining Engineers, written short

explanation.walkthrough: 'Take off' is mimicry, not lifting off; the second sense is the letters a member of the mining engineers' institution puts after their name.
explanation.definitionFit: A mimic's act imitates others, and the same letters abbreviate a member of the Institution of Mining Engineers.

clue.text: Transfer-paper ?

definitions.meaning: in law, the handing over of a right or property to another person
a piece of set work, such as an essay given to a student

explanation.definitionFit: Legally it is the conveyance of property or rights, and in school it is a set task or written paper.
